job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work as a junior web developer at a small agency in Preston that builds websites for local shops and a few charities. I started in July, so about four months, on a graduate contract. I studied software engineering at the university here, passed with an average mark and didn't manage a placement. Most days I fix layout problems and update plugins on old sites, and the boss Gary (the owner of the agency) sends me emails with 'quick tweaks' that take half a day. I share a house with two lads from church, which keeps the rent down. I go to church on Sundays and I help with the youth group on Wednesdays. I've never used an AI tool, and I intend to keep it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've thought all along, that people get carried away. At work I'd tell Gary it won't change much for us, because our customers want a person to ring. To the lads at church I'd say the old ways usually win out. I'm not online much, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I carry on the same, which is not great but at least I know it. My wage is low and my loan is huge, and I haven't got anything saved except a couple of hundred. The agency's tiny, six people, and if Gary loses two clients we're in trouble. That's got nothing to do with AI and everything to do with a small firm in a town with few tech jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard, because that's how you hold on to a job. I'd pick up extra work from Gary, even small fixes on weekends if he'd pay. I'd cut what I spend on, which isn't much anyway. And I'd keep helping at the youth group, because it matters to me more than the job does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, which I'm grateful for. A bit worried about the loan, but I'm used to that. I'd say I'm managing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gary's 'quick tweak' look like, and does it bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it was, make the logo bigger on all pages, and it turned out the logo was baked into the template in six different places. Half a day, no thanks, no extra. It bothers me, but I don't say anything. You don't complain to the man who gave you the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take weekend work from Gary if he'd pay. Would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask once, politely. If he said no, I'd leave it. I don't like to push, and I'd feel I was ungrateful. My dad's a roofer and he always said, do the job properly and the work comes to you. I still believe that, mostly.

say: I'd say people get **carried away**, and our customers want a person to ring.
I'd tell the lads at church the old ways usually **win** out.
think: I carry on much the same, with a low wage, a huge **loan** and a couple of hundred saved.
The agency has six people, so two lost **clients** would put it in trouble.
do: Work hard and keep my head down to hold the **job**.
Ask Gary for paid **weekend** fixes, once.
Keep helping at the church **youth group**.
feel: Steady and grateful, a bit worried about the **loan**.
S0.quote: You don't complain to the man who gave you the job.
fieldNote: He is anxious about the **agency's** size, not AI, which he dismisses with old-ways confidence.
Duty and gratitude stop him asking for credit or pay.
The youth group is where he places his sense of worth.

steps.text: Ask Gary once for paid weekend fixes on client sites
Keep fixing layouts and updating plugins on the agency's old sites
Cut my spending to church, rent, food and the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sceptical, but I can see it's changing things. At work I'd tell Gary that our customers don't want a robot designing their shop's site. To the lads at church I'd say it's one more thing that makes people lazy. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's going to hit the work I do. Gary's already showing us websites made by a tool in ten minutes, and some of them are decent. If customers can get that for nothing, why pay the agency? I'd be one of the first to go, since I'm the newest and not the best. I'm afraid of it, and it makes me cross, because I did everything I was told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder and try to look useful in the ways a tool can't, like visiting the customers in person. I'd learn a bit about the tool, if I had to, though I really don't want to. I'd ask my uncle Raymond, who runs an electrical business, if there's work for me in the evenings. And I'd cut my phone, my streaming and any trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being told the way you've always done things is wrong. I'm angry and a bit ashamed. I'd say it's mostly worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tool if you had to. What would 'had to' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary saying, from Monday, we use this or we close. Then I would, grudgingly, because I need my wage. I wouldn't be good at it. I like knowing how a thing works inside, and these tools are like a sealed box. I'd probably get a lad from church to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle's business offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raymond does house wiring and fire alarms in Chorley. He'd let me carry cables and learn on Saturdays, unpaid at first, paid later maybe. He's said so more than once. I'd be useful there, and the work isn't going to be done by a machine soon.

say: I'd tell Gary our customers don't want a **robot** designing their shop's site.
think: It will hit my work, because tools make decent sites in **ten minutes**.
I'd be one of the first to go, since I'm the **newest** and not the best.
do: Visit customers in **person**, which a tool can't do.
Ask my uncle Raymond for evening **electrical** work.
feel: Angry and a bit **ashamed**, like being told the way I've always worked is wrong.
S1.quote: I like knowing how a thing works inside, and these tools are like a sealed box.
fieldNote: He expects to be **cut** because the agency's own boss shows tool-made sites.
His anger is about being told to change after doing what he was told.
Uncle Raymond's electrical work is a real hands-on way out.

steps.text: Visit client shops in person to keep their business
Learn house wiring from my uncle Raymond on Saturdays
Cancel streaming and the phone contract upgrade
Look for electrical trainee jobs in Chorley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not a warning, it's an ambush. At work I'd ask Gary what we do, and I suspect he'd say he doesn't know. To church people I'd say we need to look after each other and not leave anyone behind. Online I wouldn't speak, but I'd vote for whoever could keep jobs for people who work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the work I trained for ends before I've even got going. Two years is short, and I'm a slow learner with new things. I'd have the loan hanging over me for years with no job to pay it. I'm thinking about my girlfriend Hannah too, because we'd planned to get engaged next year. I don't know if I can ask her, with nothing behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move on to hands-on work as fast as I can, because robots take until about 2031. I'd ask Raymond for a proper trainee job, even at a low wage. I'd postpone the engagement. I'd lean on the church, because people there have helped others find work and meals. And I'd cut every cost except rent, food and the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing in a field and watching a storm come across. I'm frightened. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd feel a bit less alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off the engagement. How would you tell Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with her on a Sunday, after church, and say it plainly. I'd say I want to marry my girlfriend Hannah and I want to do it right, and I need a bit of time to get steady. She's practical. She might cry. But she'd rather hear it from me than find out later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does leaning on the church look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Whitfield (a church elder) runs a fund for members out of work. There's a Tuesday lunch where people swap contacts. I'd tell the elders early, not when I'm drowning. I'd be embarrassed, but I've watched them help others, so I know it works.

say: I'd say two years isn't a warning, it's an **ambush**, and I'd ask Gary what we do.
I'd tell church people to look after each other and leave **no one** behind.
think: The work I trained for ends before I've **got going**, and I'm slow with new things.
I may not be able to ask Hannah to **marry** me with nothing behind me.
do: Move to **hands-on** work fast, starting with a trainee job with my uncle Raymond.
Lean on the **church** and cut everything except rent, food and the loan.
feel: Like standing in a field watching a **storm** come across, frightened, but less alone when I pray.
S2.quote: I want to marry my girlfriend Hannah and I want to do it right, and I need a bit of time to get steady.
fieldNote: The 2-year window removes his **plan** and threatens a personal one: his engagement.
He knows he is a slow learner and says so plainly.
Faith and community are his real safety net; he'd tell elders early.

steps.text: Ask my uncle Raymond for a proper trainee electrician job
Tell Hannah on a Sunday that the engagement waits a year
Tell the church elders early and use the members' fund
Cut every cost except rent, food and the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair bit of notice and people should use it. At work I'd tell Gary we should train for work that needs a person on the spot. To church I'd say, teach the young ones a trade as well as a screen. Online, I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried but I'm not panicking. I think I could retrain by then, if I start. I'd rather do honest work with my hands than argue with a machine. I'd probably have to change my plans, but five years lets me do it in order. I'd still like to marry Hannah, buy a small house and have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start on evenings and Saturdays with Raymond, and get a proper electrical qualification. I'd save £60 a month. I'd stay at the agency while I trained, as long as they kept me. And I'd marry Hannah in the church next summer, quietly, with a small do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bearable. I think it's about having a plan with a date on it. I'm still a bit nervous, but I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry next summer rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we've waited long enough, and we're going to be poor either way. Two can live more cheaply than one. And I don't want to hold up my life for the sake of a risk I can't measure. If I'm going to be working with my hands, I might as well do it with a wife beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the agency make of you training as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary would think I was leaving, and he'd be right in the end. I'd tell him early, and I'd do the job until he found someone. I'd want him to say, he left properly. That matters to me.

say: I'd say five years is fair **notice** and Gary should train for work that needs a person on the spot.
I'd tell church to teach the young a **trade** as well as a screen.
think: I'm worried but not panicking, and I'd rather do honest work with my **hands**.
Five years lets me change my plans **in order**.
do: Train evenings and Saturdays with Raymond for an electrical **qualification**.
Marry Hannah in the **church** next summer, quietly.
feel: Bearable, because a plan with a **date** lets me sleep.
S3.quote: I don't want to hold up my life for the sake of a risk I can't measure.
fieldNote: A **dated plan** calms him; faith and family shape each step.
He tells the boss early and wants to leave well.
He is still anxious, since the new trade pays little at first.

steps.text: Train with my uncle Raymond on evenings and Saturdays
Save £60 a month towards the wedding and a cushion
Marry Hannah at the church next summer
Stay at the agency while I train, and tell Gary early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we shouldn't waste it. At work I'd say let's keep the agency personal and local. To church I'd say to look after the old and the young, whatever comes. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is enough to settle. I'd be married, with a bit of a house, and I could be a qualified electrician by then. I don't think the machines will wire a house for a long while, and people will always need heat and light. I'm slightly worried that I'll resist change too long out of habit, but I also think that being stubborn has its uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical qualification gradually while keeping the job, and get fully qualified in about four years. I'd save for a deposit. I'd keep up the youth group and maybe teach them a bit about trades. And I'd try to use the AI a little, if only to know what I'm complaining about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, even good. There's time, and that takes the pressure off. I'd say I'm hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being stubborn has its uses. Give me an example.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was nineteen, a lecturer told me to drop a module because it was hard. I didn't, and I passed it with a decent mark. But I also ignored good advice from time to time. So it's a mixed blessing, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your own children about all this one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to do something real with your hands and keep your faith and your family close. And don't borrow so much for a certificate. I'd help them where I could, which I couldn't have, so I'd want to be able to.

say: I'd say ten years is long and we shouldn't **waste** it.
I'd tell church to look after the old and the **young**.
think: Ten years is enough to **settle**, married with a bit of a house.
I may resist change too long out of **habit**, but stubbornness has uses.
do: Complete an electrical **qualification** in about four years while keeping the job.
Try AI a little, **just** to know what I'm complaining about.
feel: Fine, even good, because time takes the **pressure** off.
S4.quote: I'd say learn to do something real with your hands and keep your faith and your family close.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his **fear** into a settled plan with family and faith at its centre.
He half-accepts trying AI, framed as knowing what he opposes.
His worry about borrowing for children's education is concrete.

steps.text: Finish an electrical qualification in about four years
Save for a house deposit with Hannah
Try an AI tool once a week to see what it does
Teach the church youth group about trades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It would take away the work I trained for before I'd got going, and I'd have a loan with nothing behind it. What would help is a trade apprenticeship that actually pays, an employer who tells me straight, and people around me. For me that's the church and my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people my age aren't lazy and we're not asking for handouts. We borrowed to do what we were told was the sensible thing. I'd like a fair chance to work. If a person is willing to graft, there should be a place for them.

headlineQuote: If a person is willing to graft, there should be a place for them.
portrait: Zane is a 22-year-old software engineering graduate working as a **junior web developer** at a six-person agency in Preston.
He is traditional and resistant: he has never used AI and prefers knowing how things work.
His church, his girlfriend Hannah and his uncle Raymond's electrical business are his **real** safety net.
He is anxious when little changes because the agency is tiny, and panicked at two years.
He would rather graft with his hands than take handouts, and plans around marriage.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it threatens his work, his loan and his plans to marry.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship**, a straight-talking employer, and the support of his church and family.
